hints: You don't need to know the exact path. As you walk the stones left to right, what single number tells you how far the frog could possibly get so far?
Greedy: keep farthest, the furthest stone reachable using stones seen so far. If you ever stand on a stone beyond farthest, the frog is stuck.

1. farthest = 0.
  2. For i from 0 to n−1: if i > farthest, return false.
  3. farthest = max(farthest, i + stones[i]).
  4. If farthest ≥ n−1, return true.
  5. Return true after the loop.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Recursively try every hop length from every stone.

approaches.name: Better
approaches.idea: DP from the back: stone i is good if some stone within its hop range is good.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: One pass tracking the farthest reachable index.

explain: Sample 1 is [1,3,0,0,2]. At i=0, farthest = 1; at i=1, farthest = 1+3 = 4, which is the last stone, so the answer is true. In sample 2 [2,1,0,0,5], farthest reaches 2 and stays 2, so at i=3 we have 3 > 2 and the frog is stuck. Every stone up to farthest is reachable, because you can always hop shorter than the maximum. A single stone array is trivially true.
recognize: Each element is a maximum jump length and you only ask 'can I reach the end?' → track the farthest reachable index greedily.
